scenario: A 31-year-old previously healthy woman was referred to the uveitis service for evaluation of acute unilateral anterior uveitis with hypopyon and an iris lesion. She reported 1 day of right eye pain and blurred vision, without photopsia or floaters. She had started hourly topical prednisolone acetate, 1%, 24 hours prior to presentation without improvement. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/50 (pinhole 20/40) OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed diffuse conjunctival injection, 4+ (>50 cells/1 × 1-mm slit beam) anterior chamber cells, 1.2-mm layered hypopyon, and an iris lesion (Figure 1). The anterior segment of the left eye was unremarkable. Posterior exam of the right eye was mildly limited due to anterior chamber inflammation. There were no obvious vitreous cells in either eye. The left eye had normal anterior segment but showed retinal hemorrhages. Further history revealed systemic symptoms—headache, fatigue, subjective fevers, and left foot erythema—that began 4 days prior. She had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection (UTI) in the emergency department (ED) the previous day and received 1 dose of intravenous (IV) antibiotics. She denied recreational IV drug use.

answer: Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED

explanation: Acute endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess (secondary to infective endocarditis) D. Perform an anterior chamber tap, administer intravitreal antimicrobials, and transfer to the ED Acute endogenous endophthalmitis is a serious complication of ocular embolic events associated with infective endocarditis. It most frequently involves the retina and choroid due to their rich vascular supply, typically presenting with chorioretinitis, vitreous cells, and haze. Infected emboli may also localize to the ciliary body and iris, causing predominant inflammation in the anterior vitreous and anterior chamber, respectively. Advanced or disseminated cases may evolve into fulminant panuveitis.1 In this patient, the focal white fibrinous iris lesion represented an iris abscess (Figure 1A). Anterior chamber inflammation was pronounced, while the posterior segment was unaffected. Roth spots in the fellow eye (Figure 2), along with fever, recent UTI, and foot cellulitis, suggested infective endocarditis. Reactive arthritis, associated with HLA-B27 in 50% to 75% of cases, may follow a UTI and may present with unilateral uveitis and/or arthritis.2Although HLA-B27 testing (choice A) is valuable to evaluate acute unilateral uveitis with hypopyon, an iris mass lesion is not characteristic. Oral ulcers and fluorescein angiography (choice B) would evaluate for Behçet disease. Behçet uveitis may present with hypopyon and retinal hemorrhages related to retinal vasculitis,3but it is often bilateral and relapsing. Asking about tattoos and ordering chest computed tomography (choice C) may reveal sarcoidosis or tattoo-associated uveitis with iris nodules; however, these rarely present with hypopyon, and iris nodules should be distinguished from abscesses.4,5 Infective endocarditis, most often due to staphylococcal species, may first present with ocular signs.6Risk factors include valve disease, diabetes, poor dentition, recent surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use.6The Modified Duke Criteria incorporate microbiology and clinical features to establish the diagnosis.7Endogenous endophthalmitis may be the initial or sole manifestation of endocarditis, particularly in younger or immunocompetent patients.8 Iris abscesses are uncommon and can be easily missed without careful examination. Reported cases have been linked to intravenous drug use, although this patient denied this risk factor.9 The patient underwent anterior chamber paracentesis with intravitreal vancomycin and ceftazidime injections. Blood cultures grew methicillin-sensitiveStaphylococcus aureus(MSSA), and aqueous cultures were negative. Echocardiography showed no vegetations or structural abnormalities, except for mild pericardial effusion. Nevertheless, a clinical diagnosis of infective endocarditis was made using the Modified Duke Criteria based on positive blood cultures for MSSA (major criterion), along with fever and immunologic or vascular phenomena, including Roth spots, iris abscess, and cellulitis (minor criteria).7 The patient completed 2 weeks of IV oxacillin and 4 weeks of IV cefazolin. Ocular management included topical moxifloxacin, atropine, and prednisolone acetate. Uncorrected VA recovered to 20/20 both eyes, with mild focal superotemporal iris atrophy in the right eye. She remained recurrence-free at 3 years. This case highlights a presentation of endogenous endophthalmitis with an iris abscess, which may be easily overlooked, as it may not be a widely recognized clinical sign among ophthalmologists. The authors emphasize the importance of careful bilateral anterior and posterior segment evaluation in unilateral uveitis with hypopyon.
